topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; competency frameworks may have limited direct application to non-healthcare organisational settings or non-European regions.
takeaways: Review provides structured competency mapping in digital health; consider whether public health competency models (e.g., data literacy, digital tool proficiency) could be adapted for your organisation's AI capability-building program.
European focus means recommendations may reflect EU regulatory context (GDPR, digital governance); verify applicability to Australian workplace regulations and organisational needs before adoption.

Scoping review format synthesises existing frameworks rather than testing effectiveness; use findings to identify gaps in your current AI literacy curriculum, but supplement with empirical validation specific to your workforce.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education curriculum design. Findings may not generalise directly to other health professions or non-healthcare fields, though the competency framework methodology could be adaptable.
takeaways: Consider developing role-specific AI competency frameworks for your organisation using similar structured approaches — identify core skills, knowledge areas, and proficiency levels relevant to your sector rather than adopting generic frameworks.

Dental education's integration of AI into existing curricula provides a model for embedding AI literacy into professional training: map AI applications to actual job tasks and clinical/operational scenarios your employees encounter.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education framework development, which may have limited applicability to adult workplace AI literacy programmes. Geographic scope and validation context not clear from title/snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-technical audiences benefits from embedding AI concepts within a broader digital literacy framework rather than teaching AI in isolation — consider mapping AI capabilities training to existing digital skills programmes in your organisation.

Middle school frameworks offer design principles for scaffolding AI concepts (e.g., starting with foundational digital competencies before advanced AI topics) that could inform how you structure AI upskilling pathways for employees with varying technical backgrounds.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global case studies and client work, but specific geographic focus and sample composition are unclear from the snippet. Findings may reflect perspectives of large, advanced organisations more than SMEs or regional variation.
takeaways: AI adoption requires simultaneous workforce capability building; treating technical implementation and people development as separate workstreams will undermine transformation outcomes.

Assess your current workforce's AI literacy baseline and identify critical skill gaps by role — prioritise upskilling pathways for roles most impacted by AI integration rather than attempting organisation-wide training.
Embed change management and psychological safety practices early in AI rollout to help employees understand their evolving roles and reduce resistance or skill anxiety.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on faculty development within public health education contexts, likely US-based given Frontiers journal conventions. Applicability to Australian organisational settings and non-academic sectors requires consideration of different regulatory frameworks and institutional structures.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption can be reframed as a readiness challenge — targeted professional development addressing specific concerns and skill gaps is more effective than mandates.
Institutional AI literacy programs should begin with educator upskilling; employees are more likely to engage with AI tools when their leaders and trainers model confidence and competence.
Structured faculty development pathways (rather than one-off workshops) help shift mindsets from viewing AI as a threat to seeing it as a capability-enhancing tool.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited without seeing full content — appears to be a higher education-focused review. Generalisability to organisational training contexts depends on how transferable academic AI competency frameworks are to workplace settings.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are foundational (e.g., literacy vs. technical skill) so you can design targeted development pathways rather than one-size-fits-all training.
Consider integrating AI competency development across multiple modes (curriculum redesign, short courses, capstone projects) rather than relying on single-delivery mechanisms.
Map competency frameworks from higher education to your workplace context — some academic outcomes may need adaptation for your specific industry and employee roles.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework applying the Automation–Augmentation Paradox to AI contexts, but generalisability depends on underlying empirical evidence base, which is not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Understand the dual risk: generative AI can either automate away employees' knowledge-building opportunities (reducing skill depth) or augment their learning by handling routine tasks—design implementation to favour augmentation by intentionally preserving learning-critical activities.

Monitor for 'deskilling' effects by tracking whether employees using AI tools show declining knowledge retention or reduced problem-solving independence; implement guardrails such as requirement to explain AI-generated outputs before adoption.

Frame AI adoption conversations around knowledge development, not just efficiency gains—employees who understand how to work *with* AI rather than defer to it are more likely to build rather than erode professional expertise.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be limited by geographic and cultural context — paternalistic leadership is more prevalent in certain cultures (e.g., East Asia) and may not generalise equally to Western hierarchical norms. Full assessment requires access to study methodology and sample details.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — when staff feel a sense of ownership over AI systems, they are more likely to actively shape and adapt them (AI crafting), leading to better collaboration rather than resistance.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, managers should explicitly support employee agency in customising AI workflows to individual needs; this bridges the gap between top-down AI implementation and genuine employee buy-in.
Use structured AI crafting opportunities (e.g., configuration workshops, customisation time) as a mechanism to build both psychological ownership and collaborative human-AI working relationships.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises research on AI's cognitive and skill impacts, but APA publications often reflect US academic perspectives; applicability to Australian workplace contexts depends on specific evidence cited.
takeaways: Identify which cognitive skills are being augmented vs. replaced by AI in your organisation, then design targeted development programs to strengthen uniquely human capabilities (creativity, complex reasoning, interpersonal skills) that remain competitive advantages.

Proactively address potential shifts in how employees think and approach problems as AI tools become embedded in workflows—consider psychological safety initiatives to help people experiment with new AI-augmented work practices without fear of looking incompetent.

Use findings on skill reshaping to shape recruitment and onboarding: prioritise candidates with learning agility and metacognitive awareness rather than static technical skills, since the skills landscape will continue shifting.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on observations from organisational contexts but lacks empirical data or specific geographic scope. Insights likely apply broadly to knowledge workers in developed economies with AI tool access, but specific risks may vary by role, sector, and organisational policy.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational policies on which AI tools employees can use for personal support (mental health, financial advice, etc.) to mitigate risks of unreliable guidance and data privacy breaches.

Provide education to staff on AI limitations — particularly that conversational AI cannot replace professional counselling or expert advice — and ensure access to proper support channels (EAP, financial advisors) remains visible and encouraged.

Monitor for over-reliance patterns in your team (e.g., employees substituting AI for peer support or professional help) and create psychological safety to discuss concerns about AI use without judgment.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from snippet alone — geographic scope and sample characteristics are not provided. Generalisability depends on whether the study involved single or multi-country samples and the sectors/roles represented.
takeaways: Role ambiguity and self-efficacy operate as distinct psychological mechanisms affecting how employees adopt and collaborate with generative AI — addressing uncertainty about AI responsibilities may require different interventions than building confidence in AI skills.

Design onboarding and role clarity initiatives that explicitly define employee responsibilities alongside AI capabilities to reduce role ambiguity, which may otherwise inhibit productive AI-human collaboration.

Assess and build employee self-efficacy with generative AI tools through structured skill-building and early wins, as confidence in one's ability to work effectively with AI independently predicts engagement with these tools.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings specific to nursing profession and medical AI contexts; generalisability to other healthcare roles or non-healthcare sectors unclear without full article details. Sample size and geographic scope would affect broader applicability.
takeaways: To support nurse wellbeing during AI adoption, prioritise preserving and expanding work autonomy rather than treating AI implementation as purely a technical change — autonomy acts as a protective mechanism against potential wellbeing risks.

When introducing medical AI systems, assess and map current autonomy levels in workflows; design implementations that maintain or enhance nurses' decision-making authority, not just add AI tools alongside existing tasks.

AI readiness programmes should include psychosocial elements addressing autonomy and control, not just technical training — this dual approach is more likely to improve adoption outcomes and staff wellbeing simultaneously.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are broadly applicable across sectors, but lack empirical validation or specific geographic scope; findings reflect consultant experience rather than rigorous research.
takeaways: Shift change management focus from AI tool adoption to behavioural adaptation: design interventions that help people develop new ways of working with AI, not just training them on features.

Use a structured change approach tailored to AI (beyond standard change management): identify key behavioural barriers specific to AI use in your context, then systematically address them through leadership, culture, and role-specific support.
Build sustained capability by embedding AI-related behaviours into team norms and workflows early, rather than treating AI adoption as a one-off training event.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope, which are not provided in the title or snippet.
takeaways: Employee job crafting responses to AI awareness operate through two distinct pathways: cognitive appraisal of stress (threat vs. challenge) and job demands-resources theory — use this dual-mechanism understanding to design targeted interventions that address both threat perception and resource allocation when introducing AI.

Interventions should focus on reframing AI as a challenge rather than a threat to shift cognitive appraisal, which may encourage adaptive job crafting (task-focused) rather than withdrawal or defensive behaviours.

Ensure adequate resources (training, autonomy, managerial support) are in place alongside AI rollout — the JD-R pathway suggests job crafting success depends on balancing increased demands with corresponding resource increases.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from a US business school with no stated empirical research base or specific sample. Findings and recommendations may not generalise beyond US-centric business contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could disrupt current roles, then design targeted upskilling programmes before implementation rather than reacting afterwards.

Engage employees early in AI transition planning to surface concerns and co-design change strategies — resistance often stems from uncertainty about job security rather than capability, so transparent communication about role evolution is critical.

Audit your current change management and learning infrastructure now to determine what additional support (mentoring, time for practice, psychological safety initiatives) will be needed to help staff adapt to AI-augmented workflows.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but lacks transparent methodology and may reflect biases toward large enterprises and sectors where McKinsey operates most heavily.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI transformation across three phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to identify which stage you're in and what capability gaps need addressing before moving forward.

Design behaviour change initiatives differently for each horizon: early adoption requires building confidence and experimentation; scaling requires standardisation and role clarity; impact requires embedding AI into decision-making cultures and workflows.

Audit whether your current change management approach supports progression through all three horizons — many organisations adopt AI tools but fail to achieve measurable business impact due to incomplete transformation of human behaviours and processes.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. Findings on job crafting responses to AI adoption may vary by sector, organisational culture, and employee demographics.
takeaways: Use the approach-avoidance framework to anticipate how your team members might respond to AI tools—some will proactively reshape their roles (approach), others may withdraw or resist (avoidance). Tailor change management to address both response patterns.

Design AI adoption initiatives that explicitly invite employees to redefine their job tasks and responsibilities, rather than imposing AI use top-down, to encourage constructive job crafting rather than avoidance behaviours.

Monitor for signs of avoidance-based responses during AI rollout (disengagement, skill development resistance) and intervene early with psychological safety measures and reskilling support to help employees embrace role adaptation.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but findings reflect clients of a major consulting firm and may skew toward large organizations with resources for transformation initiatives.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation — prioritize reskilling and role redesign alongside tool deployment to drive sustained adoption.

Identify specific job categories and workflows most affected by AI in your organization early, then design targeted change management and learning pathways for those groups rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.
Create feedback loops between frontline teams and leadership to surface real barriers to AI adoption and adjust change strategies based on what's actually blocking engagement, not assumptions.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline appears to summarise research findings without details on sample size, population, or methodology. Actual generalisability depends on the underlying study, which is not described in the snippet.
takeaways: Counterintuitively, people scoring high on antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, combative traits) may have initial romantic appeal — challenging the assumption that only grandiose charm attracts potential partners.

The 'antagonistic advantage' highlights how personality traits we typically code as negative in professional contexts can trigger attraction in romantic ones, suggesting context matters more than we assume.

This finding is a good reminder that psychological traits exist on a spectrum and don't play out the same way across different social domains — what tanks a workplace relationship might spark a romantic one.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — generalisability depends on sample characteristics, study design, and whether findings replicate across cultures and age groups, which cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Some personality types may naturally encode surprising moments more vividly than others — so your colleague's detailed memory of that awkward meeting might say something about their personality, not just their attention.
This suggests personality shapes not just what we pay attention to, but how our brains literally process and store unexpected events, making memory genuinely personal in ways beyond conscious effort.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Low — headline-driven news report with minimal methodological detail; original research source and sample characteristics unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently show structural and functional differences in psychopathic individuals, particularly in regions associated with empathy and emotional processing — a finding that's counterintuitive because it suggests neurological rather than purely behavioural roots.

The 'shocking difference' framing highlights how neuroscience keeps surprising us: what we've long assumed is purely moral choice may have measurable biological underpinnings, raising fascinating questions about responsibility and culpability.

This type of research fascinates because it sits at the intersection of biology, psychology, and ethics — it challenges our everyday intuitions about what makes someone 'bad' and whether brain differences can explain antisocial behaviour.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not specified. Findings may reflect patterns in wine review language rather than universal personality-taste relationships.
takeaways: People's wine preferences and how they describe them reveal consistent patterns linked to personality traits — suggesting our taste in what we drink isn't random, but reflects who we are.
AI can spot personality signals in everyday writing (like wine reviews) that humans might miss, revealing hidden connections between our consumer choices and psychological profiles.
Wine reviewing habits appear to be a surprisingly rich window into personality — making this a fun example of how mundane online activity can say something deeper about us.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to the twin study methodology and sample population; generalisability depends on the twin registry used and may not fully capture environmental factors that differ between twin pairs raised together.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest that authoritarian political beliefs have a measurable genetic component, challenging the assumption that ideology is purely shaped by upbringing or social environment.

The 'surprising' part: personality traits like obedience and conformity — often thought to be entirely learned — appear to have heritable foundations that predispose people toward certain political worldviews.

This finding is a good reminder that nature and nurture interact in complex ways; knowing someone's genetics doesn't predict their politics, but it does hint at psychological tendencies that might nudge them in certain directions.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Unknown — headline lacks detail on underlying research scope, sample size, or geographic focus. The actual study details are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: A surprising twist on nature vs. nurture: new evidence suggests genetics play a larger role in shaping personality than previously thought by the scientific community.

If true, this challenges the long-held assumption that upbringing and environment are the dominant forces molding who we are — counterintuitive given decades of psychology research emphasizing environmental influence.
Interesting for anyone curious about why siblings raised in the same household can be completely different people, or why personality seems to 'show up' so early in childhood.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from title and snippet alone; likely limited to specific organisational context(s) studied. Generalisability depends on sample size, industry sector, and geographic distribution of participating teams — information not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Leaders who combine inclusive practices with lower power distance orientation (reducing hierarchical barriers) create stronger psychological safety, which directly enables team innovation — consider auditing your own leadership style on both dimensions.

Psychological safety acts as a measurable mechanism linking leadership behaviour to innovation outcomes; use this framework to diagnose whether your team's innovation challenges stem from safety deficits rather than capability gaps.
Power distance orientation matters: teams led by leaders who actively flatten hierarchy alongside inclusive communication may see greater innovation gains than teams receiving inclusion alone.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but dependent on PwC's survey methodology and sample composition — typically skewed toward professional/corporate workers in developed economies. Results may not represent frontline workers, informal sectors, or lower-income countries equally.
takeaways: Identify specific workforce anxieties revealed in the survey (e.g., job security, AI impact, workload) and assess which resonate most with your organisation — this creates targeted entry points for psychological safety interventions rather than generic approaches.

Use the global hopes/fears benchmarks to frame internal conversations about change and uncertainty; acknowledging shared concerns across workforces can normalise vulnerability and reduce isolation, both key to building psychological safety.

Cross-reference any AI-related fears with your current AI capability development initiatives — misalignment signals may indicate the need for clearer communication, upskilling pathways, or reassurance about role security to strengthen trust.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample characteristics, which are not detailed in the snippet. The findings on psychological safety and ethical leadership as mediators between AI adoption and depression may apply broadly to organisations implementing AI, but sector, geography, and organisational context limitations cannot be assessed from this snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health; prioritise psychological safety and ethical leadership practices during implementation to mitigate depression and related harms.

Leaders should actively model ethical AI use and create environments where employees feel safe raising concerns about AI systems—absence of these protective factors may amplify negative psychological outcomes.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific research methodology, sample characteristics, and organisational contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Leaders can use psychological safety as a deliberate lever to reduce hierarchical barriers and enable quieter or lower-status employees to contribute ideas and voice concerns without fear of embarrassment or retaliation.

Creating psychological safety requires consistent modelling of openness to feedback, admitting mistakes, and responding non-defensively when employees raise issues — this signals safety more effectively than policy statements alone.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on HBR editorial perspective rather than empirical research. Likely reflects experiences in larger US/Western organisations but generalisability to Australian workplaces, smaller firms, or non-English contexts unclear.
takeaways: Identify and address the specific fears driving non-disclosure of AI use (e.g., fear of job loss, performance scrutiny, or policy violation) through open dialogue — employees won't self-report unless they trust the outcome will be constructive rather than punitive.

Establish explicit, written norms around acceptable AI use and create safe channels for employees to ask questions or report uncertainty before they use tools — transparency requires clarity about what's permitted, not just culture-building alone.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — Deloitte report with unspecified sample size and geographic scope. Findings likely reflect consulting firm perspective and may not generalise across all sectors or organisational contexts.
takeaways: Prioritise developing human capabilities (communication, collaboration, emotional intelligence) alongside technical skills to build psychological safety, as these are foundational to team performance rather than secondary to task execution.

Use team capability assessment to identify gaps in interpersonal skills and resilience; targeted development in these areas may improve psychological safety more effectively than structural or process changes alone.
